summary: The backend's real-time layer. `LiveHub` pushes messages to every browser connected to the Server-Sent Events stream (served by `iip/routes/system.py`, consumed by `web/js/core/live.js`), and `TrafficGenerator` is an optional background task that feeds realistic activity through the same `process_event` pipeline the REST API uses. The routes in `events.py`, `incidents.py` and `simulation.py` call `broadcast` or `hub.publish` after they change data, and `iip/app.py` binds the hub to the event loop at startup and stops the generator at shutdown.

notes.text: Module docstring, first half. It introduces `LiveHub`, the fan-out hub for the Server-Sent Events (SSE) stream, and states the key design point: `publish` may be called from worker threads (sync FastAPI endpoints run in a thread pool), so it hands each message to the event loop with `call_soon_threadsafe`.

Second half of the docstring: `TrafficGenerator` is an optional background task that produces a steady trickle of normal activity with the occasional attack, so a demo dashboard keeps moving even when nobody is clicking.
Postpones evaluation of type hints: they are kept as strings instead of being evaluated when the module is imported, which keeps imports cheap and lets hints mention names defined later.
`asyncio` provides the event loop, queues and tasks this module is built on; `itertools` supplies `count`, used to number SSE messages.
`json` serialises message payloads, `logging` reports failed traffic ticks, and `random` drives the traffic generator's choices and timing.
`AsyncIterator` is the type of the async generator `stream`, `suppress` is a context manager that silently ignores the listed exceptions, and `datetime` is used in type hints.
SQLAlchemy's `select` builds queries, and `Session` is the database-session type used in `broadcast`'s signature.
`run_in_threadpool` runs an ordinary blocking function on a worker thread and lets the calling coroutine `await` the result, so slow database work never freezes the event loop.
Project imports: `rules` (for the rapid-transaction window), the shared `utcnow` clock, and the ORM models plus `SessionLocal`, the factory that opens database sessions.
`metrics` is the shared observability registry (used to count ingested events) and `process_event` is the single write pipeline every event goes through: normalise, enrich, score, store, correlate.
`event_dict` and `incidents_page` serialise rows into the same JSON shapes the REST API returns, and the `seed` helpers generate attack scenarios and routine events for the traffic generator.
A named logger, so log lines from this module are labelled `iip.live`.
`LiveHub` keeps track of every connected browser and delivers each published message to all of them.
The constructor; `queue_size` caps how many undelivered messages each client may have waiting (256 by default).
The server's asyncio event loop. It starts as `None` and is filled in by `bind()` once the app is running.
One `asyncio.Queue` of ready-to-send SSE strings per connected browser. A set makes adding and removing a client cheap.
Remembers the per-client capacity for when `stream()` creates a new queue.

An endless counter (1, 2, 3...) that numbers every message for the SSE `id:` field; `next()` on it is atomic in CPython, so ids stay unique even when several threads publish at once. (Browsers echo the last id back as `Last-Event-ID` when they reconnect, but this server does not replay missed messages.)
`bind` stores the running event loop. `iip/app.py` calls it once at startup (`hub.bind(asyncio.get_running_loop())`) so worker threads later know which loop to hand messages to.
A read-only property: the number of connected SSE clients is simply the number of queues. The health and metrics endpoints report it as `live_clients`.
`publish` sends one message of type `kind` (`event`, `incident`, `traffic` or `reset`) with a JSON-serialisable `data` payload to every connected client. It is safe to call from any thread.
Returns immediately when no loop is bound yet (in unit tests, or before startup) or when nobody is listening, so the payload is not even serialised.

Builds the SSE wire format: a few `field: value` lines ended by a blank line (`\n\n`). `id:` numbers the message, `event:` names its type so the browser's matching `addEventListener` handler fires, and `data:` carries the JSON, which `json.dumps` writes on a single line (a raw newline would end the field) with `default=str` turning values such as datetimes into strings.
If the server is shutting down and the loop is already closed, `call_soon_threadsafe` raises `RuntimeError`; `suppress` ignores it, because a message nobody can receive is safe to drop.

The thread-safety trick. asyncio queues may only be touched from the event loop's own thread, but `publish` is often called from thread-pool workers (sync endpoints, the traffic tick). `call_soon_threadsafe` adds `_fan_out(message)` to the loop's to-do list and wakes the loop, so the queue writes happen safely on the loop thread.
`_fan_out` always runs on the event loop thread (scheduled by `publish`) and copies one message into every client's queue.
Iterates over a snapshot (`list(...)`) of the set, a defensive habit so a client connecting or disconnecting can never cause a "set changed size during iteration" error.
A full queue means that browser is not reading fast enough (slow network, a laptop gone to sleep). The comment states the policy: drop that client's oldest message rather than block everyone.
Removes the oldest waiting message with `get_nowait()`, which never waits; suppressing `QueueEmpty` is purely defensive.

Adds the new message without waiting (`put_nowait`). A slow client only loses old messages; it can never stall the publisher or the other clients, and memory stays capped at `queue_size` messages per client.

`stream` is an async generator, one per connected browser. `system.py` hands it to a `StreamingResponse`, which sends every string it yields straight to the client; `heartbeat` is the longest silence, in seconds, before a keep-alive is sent.
Creates this client's private queue, bounded to `queue_size` so a stalled client cannot grow memory without limit.
Registers the queue so `_fan_out` starts delivering to it; from now on `clients` counts this browser.
Opens a `try` so the matching `finally` always runs, however the stream ends.

The first chunk the browser receives. `retry: 3000` tells `EventSource` to wait 3 seconds before reconnecting if the connection drops, and `: connected` is an SSE comment (lines starting with a colon are ignored by the browser) that gets data flowing before any real event exists.
Loops for as long as the browser stays connected.

Waits for the next message, but for at most `heartbeat` seconds; when one arrives it is yielded, which writes it to the HTTP response. On timeout `asyncio.wait_for` cancels the pending `queue.get()`, so no message is lost.
Fifteen seconds without a message: sends `: keep-alive`, another comment the browser ignores. It stops proxies, load balancers and browsers from closing what looks like an idle connection.

When the browser disconnects, Starlette cancels the streaming task and the cancellation surfaces inside this generator (normally while it waits on the queue). The `finally` block then unregisters the queue, so disconnected clients never leak.
One module-level hub shared by the whole process: `app.py` binds it, the routes publish to it and the `/stream` endpoint subscribes to it.
`broadcast` is the helper every ingestion path calls after processing events; `source` labels where they came from (`api`, `simulation` or `traffic`) so the UI can tell them apart.
Docstring: publish the new events plus every incident they touched.
Publishes one `event` message per event, serialised with the same `event_dict` the REST API uses, so the browser can treat live and fetched data identically.
A set comprehension collecting the distinct incidents these events belong to; events that were not correlated into any incident have `incident_id` `None` and are skipped.
If any incident changed, loads them all with a few batched queries via `incidents_page` and publishes each as an `incident` message, so open dashboards can update incident rows and counters.
`TrafficGenerator` produces synthetic live activity on demand; it is switched on and off through `POST /api/v1/simulation/traffic`.
The constructor: `attack_ratio=0.06` means roughly 6% of ticks replay an attack scenario instead of ordinary activity.
Running total of generated events, shown in the status payload.
When the current run started; `None` until the first start.
Handle to the background asyncio task, used to check, cancel and await it.
The tick currently running in a worker thread, if any, so `stop()` can wait for it to finish.
Each user's last generated transaction time, so the generator can avoid unrealistically frequent transactions (see `_tick`).
`running` is true only while a task exists and has not finished; a task that was cancelled or crashed counts as stopped.
`status()` returns the small dict shared by the API and the SSE `traffic` messages: whether it is enabled, how many events it produced, and the start time (only while running).

Declared `async` even though it awaits nothing: `asyncio.create_task` needs a running event loop in the current thread, and an `async def` awaited by an async endpoint is guaranteed to run on the loop, not in a worker thread.
Does nothing if the generator is already running, so a double click cannot start two loops.
Records the start time with the shared naive-UTC clock.
Schedules `_run()` as a background task on the event loop and returns immediately; the name `iip-live-traffic` makes it easy to spot when debugging.
Tells every connected dashboard about the new state, so all traffic toggles update, not just the one that was clicked.
Stops the background task. Also called by the reset endpoint and by the `lifespan` in `app.py` at shutdown.

Takes the task and clears the handle **first**, so `running` reports `False` at once and a `start()` that arrives while this method waits creates a task of its own instead of being orphaned. Nothing to do if no task exists.
Requests cancellation: a `CancelledError` will be raised inside `_run` at its next `await`.
Waits for the task to actually finish, swallowing the expected `CancelledError`.

A tick may still be running in its worker thread, and threads can't be cancelled. Waiting for it means that when `stop()` returns nothing is writing to the database any more, which the reset endpoint relies on before it drops and re-seeds the tables. A failure in that last tick is still logged.
Broadcasts the stopped state to all dashboards.
The background loop that `start()` schedules.
A private random generator, so the traffic stream neither uses nor disturbs the global `random` state.
Runs until `stop()` cancels it.
Sleeps a random 1 to 2.8 seconds between ticks for a natural, uneven rhythm; `await asyncio.sleep` hands control back to the loop so SSE streams and requests keep flowing.

`_tick` does blocking SQLAlchemy work, so it runs on a worker thread via `run_in_threadpool`. The running tick is kept in `_ticking`, and `asyncio.shield` lets the loop be cancelled without abandoning that tick: a thread can't be interrupted, so `stop()` waits for it instead. Ticks never overlap, because each one is awaited before the next sleep.

A failed tick (for example a locked database) is logged with its traceback and the loop carries on. Cancellation still stops the loop, because `CancelledError` derives from `BaseException`, not `Exception`.
A finished tick is forgotten, so `stop()` only waits for one that is still running.
One unit of synthetic activity; it runs on a worker thread.
Opens a dedicated database session for this tick (sessions must not be shared between threads); the `with` block closes it afterwards.
Loads every user and picks one at random to act.
Fetches the ids of that user's trusted devices, so routine activity looks legitimate.
One timestamp for the whole tick.

With probability `attack_ratio`, plans a random scenario from `ATTACKS` (the attack, fraud and suspicious categories) ending now; the full user list is passed as the victim pool for multi-account attacks such as a password spray.
Otherwise, ordinary customer activity.
Explains the guard below: generating a transaction every few seconds for the same customer would trip the "Rapid transactions" rule and create false alarms.
Allows a transaction only if this user has not had one within `rules.RAPID_TRANSACTION_WINDOW` (10 minutes).
Builds one routine event (home city, clean IP, one of the user's trusted devices); with `allow_transaction=False` it can only be a login or a resource access.
Runs each payload through the real pipeline: `process_event` commits and returns `(event, assessment)`, and `[0]` keeps the stored `Event`. Generated traffic is scored exactly like API traffic.
Records the timestamp of any transaction just produced, which feeds the rapid-transaction guard on later ticks.
Adds to the running total shown by `status()`.
Counts the events in the per-minute ingest throughput charted on the Integration page.
Pushes the new events and any touched incidents to all dashboards. This call happens on a worker thread, which is exactly why `publish` uses `call_soon_threadsafe`.
The single generator instance, controlled by the simulation routes and stopped by `app.py` on shutdown.
